In regard to Question No. 4 (which appeared in the orders of the day yesterday as Question No. 24), in the name of Mr. Barnard, I desire to make the following observations:
In my opinion, there are only two ways in which a question can be properly, withdrawn when once it has been presented for answer in the House, that is, first by written notice by the member, putting the question, to the Clerk of the House stating that the question is withdrawn, or by the member, in his place in the House, informing the Speaker that he desired the question to be dropped or withdrawn.
In the British House of Commons the practice is that no member can ask a question in the name of another member unless upon the request of the member in whose name the question stands. (May 11th edit. p. 251.) The practice, however, in this House has hitherto not been so rigid as this, inasmuch as members have asked questions for other members under the assumption of an implied request, at least, and, in my opinion, it is not desirable that this practice should be changed.
On the subject of answers to questions the following is the practice of the British House. (See May, 251) :
A minister may, if he thinks fit, on the ground of public interest, answer a question appealing on the notice paper, although it is not asked. A minister may also, on the ground of public interest, or some other gronmd, decline to answer a question.
Having this practice in view, I think the hon. minister would be at liberty to answer the question of the hon. member even although the member did not call the same.
It was my intentionl to reframe this question, but if the hon. minister wishes to answer, I have no particular objection.

Instead of answering the question categorically I beg to read a statement on the subject prepared for me by Major-General Sir Percy Lake, chief military adviser of the government and inspector general:
In every fortress guns of various natures and power are permanently mounted in the batteries designed to protect the place, from guns of the largest calibre down to 12 pr. and 6 pr. quick-firing guns, and even machine guns. These are called its ' fixed armament,' and are mainly for use against ships and smaller vessels. Again, a certain number of guns are allotted to every fortress, as what is called ' movable armament,' i.e., mobile light guns capable of being moved about from place to place to meet attack in localities upon- which the fixed armament of the fortress could not be brought to bear. The guns to which, it is presumed, the questions refer, belong to this latter description of armament.
When Esquimalt was taken over from the British government, the ' movable armament ' which had been allotted to it was found to be one battery (6 guns) of 13-pr. muzzle loading guns. In other words, 13-pr. M. L. guns were included in its armament for use in repelling either a landing attack made outside the range of the fixed guns, or an attack from the land side of the fortress, upon which the guns of the ' fixed ' armament could not be brought to bear. For a few years after the departure of the British troops, these 13-pr. guns were retained as part of the movable armament of the fortress, but, in view of the difficulties experienced in maintaining their ammunition (which was rapidly becoming obsolete) in an efficient condition, and the drawback that this gun used ordinary gunpowder, and not smokeless, it was always intended to replace them bv 12-pr. B. L. guns firing smokeless powder, as soon as these latter should become available in consequence of the rearmament of the field artillery generally with the new 18-pr. guns.

The 12-pr. B. L. guns to which the question refers are assumed to be the battery of 12-pr. B. L. guns which has recently been sent to Victoria for this purpose.
Again, it is not correct to say that these 12-pr. guns, or indeed any guns of any nature, are ' supplied to regiments or units of garrison artillery.' All guns are supplied and belong to the fortress only, and the corps or men told off to work or drill with any particular gun may, at any time, be changed, and indeed often are changed as circumstances require. For the working of the particular guns in question, a company or part of a company of the 5th regiment, C. A., will now be detailed, probably the same company which, in previous years, has been detailed to train, and has trained, with the old 13-pr. muzzle loading guns, which have now- been taken away. The selection of the particular company or part of a company of the 5th regiment to be trained in the use of these guns will be made by the officer commanding the regiment, in communication with the officer commanding the Esquimalt defences.
It may be noted that, in the case of Halifax, the movable armament includes, and has, for many years past, included, among others, 15-pr. B. L. field guns, while this gun and the 12-pr. B. L. gun are in use for the same purpose in many of the fortified ports of Great Britain and the empire generally. It is considered that, for the special conditions of Esquimalt, 12-pr. B. L. guns are well suited, probably better suited than would be the 15-pr., inasmuch as they are lighter and more easily handled on bad roads.
Note.-The new 18-pr. field guns are nowhere allotted for this purpose.

In resuming the debate on the budget, I desire to join the felicitations of those who have already addressed the House on the character of the budget, and to extend to the hon. the Finance Minister my congratulations on the splendid statement which he has again presented to this House and to the country. The position which he occupies is certainly unique and unparalleled in the history of this country, and I think in the history of any country. Occupying, as he has, for the long period of thirteen years, uninterruptedly, the position of Finance Minister, he has been able to present to this House a succession of budgets that have at once given an indication of a growth, a prosperity and a development on national lines that has perhaps been unequalled in the history of any country. It is all the more gratifying to us to listen to such a statement in view of the recent world-wide depression that prevailed throughout the United States as well as European countries, and which was in a measure reflected in our own country, and which resulted in a certain recession of our trade, so that our revenue was somewhat less than it had been the year before. Last year the revenue was in the neighbourhood of $11,000,000 less than in the previous year. But we all rejoice that now there is every evidence of an increased revenue, and of a return of prosperity that will even surpass that of the record year of 1907-8. I have here a return for the month of December, from which I find that the optimistic forecast of which the Finance Minister. gave on the introduction of his budget, is more than likely to be fulfilled. For instance, we see that the total revenue for the month of December was $8,733,571, an increase of $1,550,216 or over 20 per cent compared with December of 1908. For the nine months, the revenue has been $73,390,008, an increase of $11,091,497. The increase in the customs revenue has been $9,361,421. If this increase for the month of December continues during the next three months of this fiscal year, there is no doubt that our revenue will exceed the $97,500,000 which the Minister of Finance estimated, and may possibly touch the $100,000,000 mark at the end of this current year. But there is also another pleasing fact about the returns. The expenditure, on the other hand, shows a decrease for the nine months of $3,034,492 on consolidated fund account, and of $2,290,206 on capital account. The total expenditure on consolidated fund account was $47,-

398,129, and on capital $24,026,137, of which about $17,000,000 was on the National Transcontinental railway. We rejoice in the return of prosperity that has come to us, and we believe that we are on the eve of a growth and a development that has not heretofore been reached in the Dominion of Canada.
Now, Sir, I do not propose to answer at any great length the speech that was delivered by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) prior to the adjournment of the debate. But there are one or two statements he made which I wish to correct, and to give some information that will show that he was labouring under a misapprehension in some of the figures that he gave to the House. I would not for a moment hint that he was endeavouring to create a wrong impression, or that he wished to prejudice the country against the methods of book-keeping that prevail the government offices; but certainly he used some very strong language for one who apparently was not able to harmonize the records as they appear in the Statistical Year-book and the Trade and Navigation returns. For instance he says that the Statistical Year-book gives, for the exports in 1896, $117,684,799, while in the Trade and Navigation returns they are given as $121,013,852.
There is that difference, I presume. I have not looked up the Year-book but have [DOT]simply taken the trade and navigation returns, from which it is easy to see how that difference occurs. For instance, the hon. gentleman has quoted the two years 1896 *and 1900 in making these comparisons of exports. For 1896 there was an estimated amount short reported, as it appears in the Trade and Navigation report, of $3,329,053, which, if added to the figure given in the Statistical Year-book would correspond exactly with the total amount that is given in the trade and navigation returns. It will be observed thaOhese two figures are given on the same page of our trade and navigation returns, no attempt is made to mislead or to falsify the accounts. The Statistical Year-book does not profess to give as complete a record as the returns published in the Trade and Navigation report. In the year 1900 there is an item ' estimated short reported $5,461,411.' That added to what appears in the Year-book would make exactly the amount which he has quoted as appearing in the trade and navigation returns. The circumstances in the other two years he has quoted are exactly the same, his figures are the same simply because there were no figures in that column ' estimated short reported.' Take the columns for imports. He says that the Statistical Year-book for 1896 gives $110,587,480, and that in the trade and navigation return the figure is $118,011,508. If he had given as
much attention to the task of ascertaining the exact facts as he appeared desirous of prejudicing the House, he would have had no difficulty in seeing that these reports are exactly correct. On pages 2 and 3 of the Trade and Navigation report he will find both the amounts to which he has referred. The figures in the Statistical Year-book are taken from the imports that come into the country for consumption only, and he quotes from the trade and navigation returns the total imports. Both are given in the Trade and Navigation report and both are correct, but, as I said, the Statistical Year-book does not profess to go into these figures as elaborately and as fully. If he wished to have the facts they are there before his eyes. I shall not refer further to the different figures which he quoted, but an hon. member is not justified in using such language as this:
But when we find a discrepancy of millions of dollars in corresponding statements given in these blue-books what must we expect to find in the other accounts? Is it a fact that we are standing on a volcano and that the statement given every year by the Finance Minister is a cooked statement?
Very 'strong language indeed, I think rather unbecoming language to be employed by a member without having made a very careful study of the accounts he proposes to criticise. I have been in the House five years and I do not think I have heard a single member question the correctness of the statements in the blue-books. The hon. member is apparently trying to create an impression in this country that there is *at least carelessness in the manner of computing the statistics published in our blue-books.
What authority is there for these estimated shortages, except a fancied authority in the mind of some official?

I presume it was impossible to get the exact returns when the statements were published, but I would call attention to the fact that from 1868 to 1900 that column appears in the trade and navigation returns. Since 1900 it has been dispensed with.
The hon. member has taken exception to the methods that have been adopted in regard to the expenditure of the public funds of the country and he objects to the maintenance of the two funds, the consolidated fund account and the capital expenditure account. If he had his way he would unite these two accounts and have but one account in which all the moneys would be written up so that if there was any surplus whatever it would appear in excess over the total expenditure of the year. Personally, I prefer to take the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) as a better critic in the matter of book-keeping. The system that has been followed by the present govern-

ment is exactly the same as that followed! by the government prior to 1896 with one exception, and that is with regard to the bounties that have been paid by this government, which have been charged to capital expenditure. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has clearlv explained the reasons for that change, and I think the reasons he has advanced are very good reasons. An expenditure made for the building up one of the great basic industries of this country is practically on a par with an expenditure in the way of a railway subsidy in helping a great public work.
However, I do not wish to quarrel with my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie). He says that the former government had a surplus in only one year during the whole eighteen years they were in power, namely 1882, but he says the present government has had surpluses in four years. If the hon. member is willing to concede that this government has done four times as well in the matter of surpluses as the former government, I suppose we need not complain. Following the system that has been adopted by the present government, as well as the preceding government, I wish to consider briefly the matter of surpluses as they appear in the records. You will find that under the former government they had a number of surpluses. There were surpluses during the financial years 1886-7, 1888-9, 1889-90, 1890-91, 1891-92, 189293, or in six years in a period of twelve years, they had small surpluses amounting in all to over $9,000,000. In the first year after the Liberals assumed the reins of power there was a deficit of $519,981.44, but the following year and from that to the present time they have had each year a substantial surplus amounting to as high as $16,000,000 in one year, and giving in all a total of surpluses amounting to $114,558,259, from which deducting the deficit of the first year youi have a total of surpluses during the Liberal regime amounting to $114,068,277.

Would he be kind enough to tell us what has become of all these surpluses?

With very much pleasure. The surpluses that have accrued to the credit of the government have been expended on capital account, and I should suppose that my hon. friend who has been in the House for a great many years would know that.
Then they were not surpluses.

They were surpluses over and above the ordinary or current expenditure. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) is too old a parliamentarian, I should judge, not to be better posted than he appears to be. He has been in the House long enough to be very well versed in the system of keeping the governmental accounts not only by this government but by the preceding Conservative government. However, he wants to know what has become of these surpluses and I have great pleasure in telling him that they have been expended on public works which stand as assets to the credit of the Dominion of Canada; not liquid assets in a sense, not interest bearing assets, but assets that indirectly contribute to the wealth and the growth and the prosperity of the country. For instance, I could give a statement of some of the expenditures that have been made from this source. Take the betterment of our canals. Does my hon. friend not consider that to be a wise expenditure on capital account; and on canals during the years of office of the present government there has been an expenditure of $28,385,227. Take again the Montreal harbour and the St. Lawrence ship channel. Who would say that is not a great national work in the interests of Canada and one which contributes immensely to the prosperity and the general welfare of our country? On improving the Montreal harbour and St. Lawrence ship channel there has been expended by this government $7,663,062. Then, in bonuses or subsidies to railways throughout the Dominion there have been expended $24,679,973; for harbours at Fort William, Port Arthur and Port Colborne there have been expended $2,276,303, and on the Quebec harbour $765,225. These are a few of the expenditures that have been made out of the surpluses to which I have already called the attention of the House. Now, I said that there had been surpluses to the amount of $114,000,000. Expenditures on capital account have been made to .the amount of $212,000,000 during the twelve and three quarter years of Liberal government. It is true that our debt has increased somewhat, and of necessity it would have to increase when we have surpluses of $114,000,000 and capital expenditure of $212,000,000, and so we have had to borrow some money to meet these extra expenditures on capital account. But,

if you deduct the expenditure on the National Transcontinental railway and the Quebec bridge amounting to $58,500,000, you will see that all the government has had to borrow during the whole, twelve and three-quarter years have been about $7,000.000. As I say, this has come from the wise management by this government of the finances of the country, so that they hail a sufficiency to meet the demands of government, apart from the National Transcontinental railway, with the exception of some $7,000,000. On the other hand, how does that compare with the record of the former government? During the whole eighteen years of their term the total expenditure of the Conservative government on capital account was $167,162,252. Did they have nearly enough money to meet that capital expenditure? No. We find that they had to borrow money, that the revenue was not sufficient to meet the current expenditure and leave any considerable amount to apply on capital account, and out of that $167,000,000 during their whole eighteen years of office they only had $49,000,000 to apply on capital account. In other words, they had to go to the English market and borrow to the extent of $118,000.000 as against the $7,000,000 that this government lias had to borrow during their twelve and three-quarter years. It will of course be said that the Conservative government built the Canadian Pacific railway. Well, eliminating the Transcontinental railway and eliminating the Canadian Pacific railway if you will, you will then see that the Conservative government had to borrow at least five times as much as the present government has had to borrow for the carrying on of the affairs of the country.
The hon. member for North Simcoe, as do many others on that side of the House, seems to think that because there is an adverse balance of trade against us it is an indication that the country is not prospering as it should. I am not very much surprised that our friends opposite sometimes think there is danger when they see an adverse balance of trade, because during their regime they had a very sad experience in that respect and perhaps it has made a very deep impression on their minds. In looking briefly into this question I find that from 1878 to 1896 the total imports were $2,044,807,768 and the total exports $1,682,592,467. There was an excess of imports over exports of $362,215,301, or an average of $20,123,000 per year for the whole 18 year period. If there had been compensating assets or sources of revenue or something to compensate for this adverse balance of trade it would not have seemed so bad, but we find that during their regime there was no material increase in population, there was no great inflow
of immigrants to the country, no great public works, apart from the C.P.R., were constructed, to stand as great assets to the country. So, I say that this adverse balance of trade was a menace, and I am not surprised that they are so much concerned when they see a small adverse balance of trade accruing under the present government. The hon. member says that there is an adverse balance of trade during the twelve years up to the present time of $202,604,892. I do not know whether his figures are correct, but I have. taken his own figures. With less than half the volume of trade, according to his figures, we have only about half the amount of an adverse balance. He says that when there is an adverse balance of trade, or even when trade is buoyant, times in the country are not so good. I take issue with him. In the first place, when trade is buoyant and is increasing rapidly, it is the best possible evidence of good times and prosperity as a whole in the country. I also take issue with him when he says that an adverse balance of trade is always a bad sign. Of course, there is a limit to which we can go with an adverse balance of trade without evil effects accruing to the finances of our country, but a small adverse balance of trade under certain conditions, is almost, I was going to say, a matter of necessity. I think I might use that expression in connection with the affairs of the country as we have seen them during the past twelve and three-quarter years. When the country is growing rapidly, when the population is increasing, when capital is coming to our shores for investment these things contribute to the increase of trade and especially do they contribute to the increase of imports. We will take, for instance, the money that has flowed into the Dominion of Canada for various purposes and see what we have as a compensating asset against this small amount of $202,000,000 which our friend says stands as an adverse balance of trade. For railway construction and for other public works it is estimated that at least $300,000,000 have come into the Dominion of Canada during the last twelve or fifteen years. The hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke), from a source that I suppose is fairly reliable, stated that at least $220,000,000 have come from the United States for investment in industrial enterprises during the last twelve years. We have had about 500.000 immigrants during the last nine years from the United States and it is estimated that last year alone the 90,148 immigrants who came into Canada from the United States brought with them, on the average, $1,000 apiece. That would amount to $90,000,000. Those that came in during preceding years, numbering, as I have said, some 500,000, less those who came

in last year, have brought in at least from $100,000,000 -to $150,000,000. Some may say that this is an exaggerated estimate. It may be somewhat large but for those who have seen the class of immigrants who are coming in from the United States, farmers who have sold their farms at good prices and many of whom have brought in from $5,000 to $20,000, it is not unreasonable to suppose that this estimate is fairly correct. So that, from this source we have had brought into the Dominion money to the extent of iabout $250,000,000. I am leaving out entirely the money that has been brought by immigrants from Great Britain and other European countries. During the last twelve years immigration from Europe has totalled about 700,000 people. Possibly they have brought in $50,000,000, perhaps more; certainly they have brought in a considerable amount of money. Added to all that, political economists tell us that every able-bodied citizen who comes into the country becomes an asset worth, at least, $1,000. If we add that to the amount I have already named, you will see that we have a compensating asset to stand against any adverse balance of trade amounting to nearly $2,000,000,000. The figures are large but still they are figures that cannot b'e gainsaid. It is a fact that stands there and it, in a very large measure, answers the question: Why is it that our banks are receiving such an immense amount in deposits? Why is it that the general prosperity of the country is so evident? It is because of this large capital which has gone into circulation, and hence I say that this money which has come in and in some cases part of it going out for the purpose of buying imports, has materially contributed to what appears to be an adverse balance of trade. We know, however, that an adverse balance of trade is the usual experience of nearly all of the great countries of the world. Great Britain, Germany, France, Holland, Italy for the last thirty years have nearly always had an adverse balance of trade. The United States is frequently referred to as a country that has an excess of exports over imports, but if you go back and look at the history of the United States you will see that from 1855 to 1873 they had an excess of imports over exports amounting to $70,000,000 annually. So, I say there is no ground for alarm; in fact, there is no reason whatever for us feeling that there is any danger from the small balance of trade that has been referred to. I wish to call your attention to a statement that was made by the Vice President of the Montreal Bank in his annual report. He says:
The adverse balance of trade has thus again begun to grow, but while men and money pour into Canada from abroad the disparity need not cause uneasiness. Domes-Mr. SCHELL.
tic industries are, speaking generally, working well up to the limit of capacity. Labour is fully employed; the lumber trade has improved. The export of dairy produce has been larger than last year, with high prices ruling throughout the season, all farm products, indeed, are exceptionally dear.
That is the view that is entertained by this high authority that I have quoted.
Now, in the matter of loans, our friends opposite seem to think that the government are not effecting loans as cheaply as they were effected under their regime. Well, possibly some of the loans are not effected as cheaply. We know that money fluctuates in the money markets of the world like any other commodity. After the Boer war, money became much dearer, and in consequence of tile increase in the rates of interest, it was not practicable, in the last few years, to renew loans on as favourable terms as in previous periods. Therefore our government as we have heard from the hen. the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) on more than one occasion, found it more difficult to replace loans as cheaply as they could a few years ago, and our Finance Minister only made loans at short terms so that he might be able to take advantage of the market when, in the natural order of things, money became more plentiful. Let me read a statement which appeared in the Toronto ' Saturday Night,' written by its financial editor, and which I think bears directly on the subject :

It may be interesting to know that while the public debt of Canada is strictly increasing, the rate of interest is decreasing. At confederation, fdrty-two years ago, the dominion paid an average rate of 5 -55 per cent on $67,069,115 which London had advanced. The interest on this which had to be remitted, either in the sale of produce or in gold, amounted to $3,700,000 yearly. After the lapse of ten years, or in 1877, the debt of the country to London had increased to $122,477,629, but the average interest rate had been scaled down to 4 -74 per cent. In the next ten years the federal debt of Canada had reached $171,075,735, while the average rate of interest had fallen to 3 -.99 per cent. This entailed the sending abroad of $7,000,000 for the payment of interest on the debt. In the next decade, ending in 1897, Canada's obligations to London had increased to $218,225,503, necessitating an annual interest of $8,125,664, but the average rate of interest had fallen to 3 -72 per cent. According to the return for the past fiscal year, our debt to London had swollen to $262,000,000, on which the interest charge will be about $9,300,000, which is at the rate of 3J per cent. In the forty-two years, therefore, of the life of the Dominion of Canada, her obligations to London in borrowings had grown from $67,000,000 to $262,000,000, an increase of $195,000,000, and while the total annual cost to the government had expanded from $3,700,000 to $9,300,000 annually, the aver-

age rate at which the borrowings had been made were reduced from 5-55 per cent, to 3-56 per cent.
There, I think is a complete answer to the contention of our hon. friends opposite that the government is not effecting loans cn as good terms as they should be able to do. A good deal of attention has been given to the average rate of duty on imnorts into Canada. Almost the only criticism of the present tariff by our opponents is levelled at the rate of duty on dutiable imports. In all their statements they totally ignore the free imports. Now, that is wholly unfair. The present government, when it came into power, declared that certain commodities should be put upon the free list. Surely, that is to be regarded as a reduction-it is a reduction to the limit. We must consider the free imports, then, if we seek to arrive at a fair idea of the tariff imposed on goods imported into Canada. We find that the total free imports from 1884 to 1896 were $457,739,263. The total free imports from 1897 to 1909, a period of equal length, were $1,108,199,713, or $650,459,950 more of free imports during the latter period than during the former. If these goods, instead of being admitted free, had been charged the average rate of duty which is now charged on dutiable goods, the Canadian people would have had to pay higher customs duties to the amount of $107,586,075.
What has that to do with it?

That shows that the government has been carrying on a policy that makes for free trade to the extent of allowing this amount of goods to come in free of tariff charge.. Or, if you wish to look at

it another way:	The total free and dutiable goods imported since 1896 amounted to $2,822,097,615, had these imports been charged at the difference between the rate of duty that obtained in 1896 and the present rate, the Canadian people would have had to pay into the Dominion treasury $71,681,279 more than they actually did pay. At this rate, as I have stated, the people of Canada would have paid over $7,000,000 more than they actually have paid on the imports since 1896.

Sydney Fisher) and his able staff of officers. I do not suppose that our friends opposite will agree with me when I say that I think we have thp best Minister of Agriculture that the Dominion of Canada has ever had. From the day that he assumed the position of Minister of Agriculture he has pursued a progressive policy. Our friends opposite sometimes say that the Dominion of Canada has not spent enough money on agriculture, and on the other hand they sometimes object because certain amounts are expended-I suppose that no matter which

policy is pursued they will find some grievance. May I call attention to one or two facts in connection with the Department of Agricultures? At confederation the staff employed under the department consisted of 23 permanent employees. To-day we have a staff of 516 of whom 246 are at Ottawa, and as the department is now organized it consists of 12 branches whose work is of the utmost importance. Among these branches we have experimental farms, the dairy and cold storage division, the live stock division, the health of animals division, census and statistics, seeds branch and other branches whose work may not come so prominently before the people. Shortly after this government assumed office, they decided to .grant to Great Britain a preference in our markets. Following the introduction of that preference as a part of the fiscal policy of the Dominion of Canada, we find that our exports increased very rapidly. I suppose that some will ask how the granting of that preference could affect the exports from Canada? In this way, that the attention of the consumers of England was called to our products in a new way. Up to that time our food products had not attained the position in the English market to which they were entitled. When the English people saw what Canada had done in the matter of preference, coupled with the work that the Minister of Agriculture was doing in placing before the English consumers our products in the very best possible condition, the people of England saw that our goods were better than they had supposed and they paid a higher price for them, So that our exports to England increased in a very rapid manner. Since 1898 when the preference was granted, they have almost doubled. In 1896 we were exporting some $66,000,000 of agricultural products to England. In each of the years 1907-8-9, our exports of agricultural products to England were in round figures $133,000,000. That has come about, as I have stated, largely by the placing of those goods upon the English market in the best possible condition. Prior to that time our system of cold storage was not what it should be, in fact we had practically no installation of cold storage on our steamships. The government, as you know, took that matter in hand, they granted a subsidy to one or two of the steamship lines, cold storage systems were installed on two or three boats, and after that system had been in operation for two or three years it was found that all the other companies, if they wished to secure a fair share of the trade of Canada in the products of the soil, had to provide a similar service. The result has been that there is not a steamship sailing from Mr. SCHELL.
Montreal, Quebec or St. John to English ports that has not a system of cold storage installed, so that ample space is offered to any exporter who mav have perishable products to export ta the European markets. vantage of all shippers of perishable goods.
As you are no doubt aware, our firm has been for over twenty years personally represented in the port of Montreal during the shipping season, and we are therefore in a position to appreciate to the full the efforts your government have made to minimize the losses to shippers caused by neglect and delay at the ports of shipment. It is not so many years ago that a walk along the docks of Montreal would disclose thousands of barrels of apples piled in the open and exposed to the effects of the weather, both hot and cold, and with only the protection of a tarpaulin, if that, and the bottom tiers often covered with mud or coal dust.

The recent concession of your government to fruit shippers of free icing of cars during transit has had a beneficial effect on the condition of the fruit arriving at port of export.

That is a very important branch. It is one of the new branches of work that this government has taken up. We know that the way that many of our packers were packing their apples had become a scandal. This government took the matter in hand and passed the Fruit Marks Act, which has been in operation now for some four or five years and any one who knows anything about the fruit trade will at once admit that the' enforcement of that Act has resulted in very great benefit to the apple trade of this country. I believe that the work is increasing. Certainly it is one which should be pushed, and everything which has been done so far only goes to prove what a vast field there is for further work in the same direction. Take the county of Oxford and let me draw attention to some herds in my own neighbourhood. There is one of eleven cows which, before the testing, produced 4,850 pounds of milk per year each. In 1908, after that operation was started, it produced 6,380 pounds. Another herd, which formerly produced 5,374 pounds each cow, increased its production to 7,243 pounds. Still another which had produced 4,360 pounds in 1903, is now producing 7,006 pounds ner cow. I could give an individual instance of a special cow which has produced as much as 20,000 pounds in the one year, but that is a very rare occurrence. There is a record of a two-year-old cow at Innerkip in the county of Oxford which gave a production of 12,227 pounds, and the weight of the butter was 452 pounds. But of course these are record figures. I have aj record of a herd of 65 cows which produced an average of 6,210 of milk each and the milk sold for practically $76 per cow. I have another herd in my mind which, I understand, has produced over 9,000 of milk per cow, and the number of cows is twenty. The milk brought in a return of nearly $100 per cow. Of course, the farmers, adopted perhaps a little better methou in the feeding and gave more intelligent attention to the care of their stock, and the result proves that this industry might easily be doubled without very materially increasing the number of cows kept. In the Dominion we have a little over 2,000,000 cows producing on an average about 3,500 pounds of milk, some make the average less, but I think if we had a correct record it would be found to be from 3,000 to 3,500 pounds a piece. If that can be increased to 5,000 or 6,000 pounds, and I believe it can, you can readily see that the dairy industry might be developed to such an extent that after supplying the whole market, which requires about $75,000,000 worth of butter, cheese and milk annually, we could export double the quantity we do now. Instead of exporting only $25,000,000 worth, we could easily double that quantity. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) deserves considerable credit for having taken this matter in hand, and I believe his officers are going to urge on the work along the lines I have indicated, and I hope for better results from year to year.
' The wealth of Canada has been inereas-



ing at an enormous rate through the wise policy of this government. I read a statement by Mr. George Parish, editor of the London ' Statist,' at a lecture given in New York .recently, in which he said that the wealth of England had increased from $20,000,000,000 in 1850 to $80,000,000,000 at present. He also said that the wealth of the United States had increased from some $10,000,000,000 in 1850 to $107,000,000,00(1- at present; that the United States had been borrowers in the world's markets to the extent of some $6,000,000,000, and that England had been lenders to the extent of $15,000,000,000 in the last sixty years.
These figures, to my mind, were very suggestive, and I wondered where Canada would come in. Of course, we are a younger country; but when we look at the accumulating wealth in our banking institutions we cannot but realize that the wealth of Canada is becoming very considerable. Hon. members who have given any attention to the statistics of banking in Canada will appreciate that statement. In 1896 the deposits in our chartered banks and savings banks were $245,000,000. The Finance Minister told us the other day that these deposits were now' $731,000,000. We find the assets of these banking institutions have increased in a similar ratio- from $350,000,000 in 1896 to considerably over $1,000,000,000 to-day. This money must certainly come from the people of this Dominion, and if they have enough money to be able tp deposit $731,000,000, it will be seen that we have enough there alone to pay the national debt, to build the National Transcontinental railway and still leave $40 for every man, woman and child in the Dominion. According to the statistics that have been furnished by the Department of Agriculture, we have $2,800,000,000 invested in farm lands in Canada. We have 26,000 miles of railway which, at an estimated cost of $30,000 a mile, would represent an investment of about $780,000,000. And we know the growth that has taken place in our manufacturing industries, from an investment of $250,000,000 in 1896 to an investment today of nearly $1,000,000,000. If you look at the assessment of our towns and cities and consider the growth of wealth reflected in these figures for Toronto. Montreal, Winnipeg and other great cities, we begin to form some appreciative idea of the growing wealth of this Dominion. This has resulted in a very large degree-not wholly, of course-from the wise and progressive policy which this government inaugurated in 1896 and has been following ever since. I realize that every honest worker in the Dominion of Canada contributes to a certain extent to this wealth and prosperity. But the government of the day, working in unison with the people of the country, are Mr. SCHELL.
helping the development of our resources and helping to build up our Canadian nationality. I hope that from the foundations which this government has laid will rise a superstructure that will ever stand as a monument to their wise and progressive policy.

Mr. Speaker, the supporters of the government of late years have made the debate on the budget an occasion for a grand eulogium of the government and all its works, and the hon. member (Mr. Schell) who has just preceded me for the space of about two hours devoted his attention almost wholly to the same purpose. It may be a very good thing as campaign literature, it may possibly be in the interests of the Liberal party in the riding of South Oxford, but I fail to see that it can be of very much service to the people of this country. In my opinion, the proper usage of parliament is that this occasion should be considered an occasion upon which members who have any criticism to offer in regard to the action of the government should offer that criticism and should make any suggestions which they believe might be in the interest of the country. And I believe that if the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Schell) had devoted a very few moments of the time he has taken up this afternoon to some little criticism-and he knows as well as any member of this House that there are many points on which the action of the government has been open to criticism -or had made any suggestion of action that they might take in the interest of the country, he might have done at least some small good by the remarks he offered to this House. It is in accordance with the view I have just expressed that I have for several years past offered a few mild criticisms of the action of the government and a few suggestions where I thought they might take action in the interest of the country. In some cases, government action has followed the suggestions I made. I do not feel inclined to take all the credit, in fact, I do not care who gets the credit so long as the country gets the benefit of the action taken. In the same spirit, I propose to offer a few criticisms this afternoon and make a few suggestions, and I intend to be as brief as I possibly can.
In the first place, I would like to say a word or two in regard to the naval programme. And at the beginning I may say that I do not intend to trespass upon the debate that is to take place on the Bill now before the House. But this is the first time the government has given us even a vague idea-and it is even yet but a vague idea-of the action which they propose to take in the expenditure for the naval defence of the country. It has been

a great disappointment to me, after the great promises which were made during the debate last March, that the government have finally come down to such a miserable proposition in regard to providing for the naval defence of Canada. What they have proposed to do is to expend some $2,719,000 a year for the protection of our commerce, our coast line, and, indeed, of our very existence as a self-governing community. When I compare with this the estimates for this purpose which have been passed in the great dependencies of Australia and New Zealand, I must say that I feel simply ashamed to call myself a Canadian. I am thankful, however, that it is generally known throughout the world that there are two parties in this country and that it is only one party that, while acknowledging that an obligation is placed upon us to take our proper, legitimate share - in the defence of the country, estimate that share at a sum of something less than $3,000,000 per year. I have some respect for those who are prepared to stand up here and declare that they recognize no obligation at all, and consequently desire to see nothing done. But I have nothing but disapprobation of the conduct of those who acknowledge the obligation, and yet make up their minds that they will simply sponge upon the taxpayers of the mother country for as many years longer as the mother country will allow them to do so.
I may also be permitted to express my amazement that, after having six months to work out the plans which the government told us they had adopted for naval defence, they come down now with a statement that they are unable to give us the slightest idea as to when they expect to be able to put a single one of their new ships into oommis-' sion, or to have one of them ready built, manned, armed and equipped so as to be of some use as a fighting factor. The Prime Minister stated yesterday they had made no estimate whatever with regard to this particular matter. We must remember that if the government finally decides that these shins aTe to be built in Canada, it will be eighteen months or two years before they can begin even to lay the keel of the first of the small ships they speak of building, and many years after that, no doubt, before these shins will be ready to he put in commission. During the whole of that time we are still to remain in the position we are now in, of practically doing nothing whatever that will be of any effectual use in the defence of the country. Is the country willing that that shall be the case? I, Sir, believe that the great mass of the people of Canada desire to see Canada doingl her duty, and doing it at once, by giving the fleet unit which the imperial authorities have asked for, and giving it immediately.
Now, turning to other points in the policy of the government as they appear in -the estimates, I desire to say a few words in regard to the Hudson Bay railway. All that appears in the estimates for the year ending March 31, 1911, is a small sum for a further survey of that route. I desire to voice my strong protest against delay in the construction of that railway. The House will remember that nearly three years ago, on the 22nd of February, 1907, the Prime Minister made a declaration that ' the time has come '-those were his words-the time has come for the construction of this railway. In June of the following year, 1908, the Minister of the Interior submitted to the House, in the Dominion Lands Act, certain provisions to create a new source of revenue adequate to build that railway- that is the language he used in explaining the provisions. The House adopted those provisions, and the funds to build the railway are now in process of being made up, and a large amount of money has already been collected in that connection. A general election was pending shortly after that time, and in -opening the campaign the Prime Minister said, in September, 1908:
' The time is now-not to-morrow but now ' that this railway should be constructed. He made a most definite promise that the construction of the Hudson Bay railway should be proceeded with, and the Liberal party waged the greater part of the election campaign in the Northwest upon that declaration. It was quoted from one end of the country to the other as a -specific promise, that if the country returned the Prime Minister to finish his work, he intended to include in that work the building of the Hudson Bay railway. Yet we find that no provision whatever has been made in the estimates for the turning of a single sod on that railway, at least up to the 31st of March, 1911. I would urge upon the Minister of Finance that he should bring down supplementary estimates to provide for this necessary work. It is an absolutely necessary work if the produce of the Northwest is to find an outlet. During the past summer a large number of resolutions in favour of the building of this railway have been passed by various public bodies throughout the Northwest ; they have doubtless all been placed in the hands of the Minister, and as some of them have been forwarded to me for my information, I propose to read one -out of a great number, all couched in about the same terms. To show the feeling of the people of the Northwest in regard to this matter, I will read a copy of a resolution passed by one of the town councils in the district I have the honour to represent:
Whereas, the development and commercial prosperity of eastern Canada are largely dependent upon the grain production and pur-

chasing power of the prairie provinces of the west, and,
Whereas, the grain and cattle carrying capacity east of the head of Lake Superior is not keeping pace with the rapidly increasing production of wheat and other exports of the w est, and,
Whereas, an amount equal to the entire cost of the Hudson Bay railway is annually expended by the west on unnecessary freight charges consequent upon the present long haul to Atlantic tide water, thus reducing the purchasing power of the west and the corresponding prosperity of the east, and,
Whereas, explorers, navigators, engineers, contractors, and others familiar with the Hudson bay route, are practically unanimous as to the practicability of the route, the easy and rapid construction of the railway, and the natural harbour facilities at Churchill.
Therefore be it resolved:
That the government of Canada be requested to get busy and build 165 miles of the Hudson Hay railway in 1910, and the remainder of the road, 160 miles from each end of the line, in 1911; and during 1910 and 1911 install the necessary terminal facilities, elevators, harbour improvements, etc., to be ready for the adequate handling of traffic not later than July 1, 1912.
The House will see how very little prospect there is of the wishes of the people of the Northwest being carried into effect, when we realize that no provision whatever is being made which will enable the construction of that railway to be comj menced for the next fifteen months. Not only have towns, villages, boards of trade, and other public bodies in the Northwest passed resolutions on this1 subject, but the legislature of Saskatchewan has passed a resolution only the other day unanimously calling upon the Prime Minister to implement the promise he made to build this railway. I spoke just now of some provision being made already for the cost which this railway is likely to involve. In reply to a question I asked the other day, thef Minister of the Interior stated that there had been a sale Of pre-emption and purchased homesteads to the extent of 4,130,400 acres of land. That answer was given last month, and covered a period up to the 31st of October last. The total sum receivable on account of these purchased homesteads and pre-emptions amounted to $12,391,200, nearly the whole amount of the money which the Minister of the Interior calculated that this railway is likely to cost. Now, I spoke on this subject last year, and again I desire to call upon the Prime Minister to implement the promise which he made. The promise was made under peculiar circumstances, but circumstances which, to my mind, involved all the greater obligation, because they gave it much more weight than the people are accustomed to attach to most promises of the ministers of the Crown. The money has been provided. The House has been led to believe that this Mr. LAKE.
construction would be gone on with as soon as that money was provided, and no criticism was offered on this side of the House with regard to the provision which it was proposed to make at that time.
I mentioned the subject of pre-emptions and I desire to urge upon the Minister of the Interior that he should not insist to the letter upon one of the provisions in regard to payment for pre-emptions and purchased homesteads. There is a provision in the law that interest should be payable yearly upon the whole amount of the obligation assumed, beginning at the end of the first twelve months. If the people' when making entries for these pre-emptions and purchased homesteads had understood this provision, I should not be so much inclined to press it on the Minister of the Interior, but I believe that very few of those applying understood that there was any such provision. I looked through the advertisements which were inserted in the newspapers announcing the sale of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads, and while all other duties were insisted upon and set out at full length, nothing whatever was said about the annual interest, which amounts to $24 per annum, further than that a gentleman who had had a demand from the department to pay this interest came to me with a couple of circulars which he had received from the department, one dated in May last. That circular called attention to the duties he would have to perform in order to earn his pre-emption. It set out all the duties of residence and cultivation but said not one word in regard to the payment of annual interest, and it was only several months later, when the first payment of interest became due, that he received a notification that there was any payment of interest to 1 be made. I think it would be found that a large number of people who in good faith made entry for these pre-emptions believed that no such payment would be demanded from them and a great number of them are not in a position to make such payments. A great deal of hardship will be caused if this is insisted upon. The Minister of the Interior told us the other day that those who did not pay would render their entries liable to cancellation. He said:
His failure to do so renders liis entry liable to cancellation.
It is a terrible position in which to place the enormous number of new settlers in that country who simply have not got this money to put up the payment of the annual interest, and I earnestly trust that the Minister of the Interior will take up this matter and will find some way out of the difficulty and not have all these homesteads liable to cancellation. I do not intend to discuss the policy by which the lands of the provinces in the Northwest are

being still retained in the hands of the Dominion government. "To my mind this great hardship must sooner or later be redressed and the provinces of the Northwest must be placed on an equality with the other provinces of the Dominion in this respect. At the same time I think it right to call the attention of the House to a development that has recently taken place and which shows the difficulties -which the retention of these lands by the Dominion government is creating. I may say that I do not consider that these questions of land in the Northwest ought to come before this House. They do not come before it in connection with the lands of any other province in Canada and yet every one of these matters has to be brought before this House and the time of this House occupied in discussing it. The lands of the different provinces, under the constitution of Canada, of right belong to the people of those provinces and they are the ones who should have the sole right to deal with them. A short time ago the statement appeared in the newspapers that the premiers of the three provinces of the Northwest, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, had asked that the administration of the school lands and the funds arising from their sale should be handed over to the provinces. I need not mention that this was a policy which was advocated by the Conservatives time and again and opposed by the Liberals, even by those who represented constituencies in the Northwest. It was put into definite shape in the year 1908 when a resolution was moved by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) from this side of the House providing:
That the Bill be not now read the third time, but be referred back to the Committee ot the Whole with instructions to amend the same by providing that, pending the transfer to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, of the Dominion lands within their respective boundaries, the school lands and all funds arising from the sale thereof, shall be handed over to the control and administration of the said respective provinces, according to their interests therein and according as the said respective provinces shall be ready to accept the same.
This resolution was voted down in this House and I regret to say with the assistance of members representing parts of the Northwestern provinces. I sincerely trust that the government will see the error of their way and will now reverse their policy in this respect, especially as the prime ministers of the two new provinces, in whose elevation to that position the government exercises such a very strong influence, are themselves now asking that this measure should be taken. I would again remind the Minister of the Interior of the necessity of providing for higher education in the new provinces, by means
of grants of land as an endowment for their provincial universities. In 1885, the Conservative administration of the day set aside 150,000 acres of land as an endowment for the university of the province of Manitoba, and I think that in consideraion of the further advance that we have made in the knowledge of the- great benefit that education is to everybody, we should not be behind hand in following such a good example and should not delay any longer in making [DOT] a considerable grant of land to the two new western universities, especially as land is being taken up so rapidly now that the time is very limited within which there is likely to be good land still available for that purpose. In the year 1908 this matter was also brought very definitely before this House in the form of a resolution moved by myself:
That the Governor in Council shall forthwith institute such proper inquiries as may be necessary for the purpose of ascertaining what quantity of Dominion lands in each of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan should be set aside and appropriated for the purposes of higher education, and that thereupon, after obtaining the consent and approval of the governments of the said respective provinces the Governor in Council shall set aside, appropriate and transfer, to the said respective provinces the quantities of said lands so ascertained for the purposes aforesaid.
That resolution also was voted down by gentlemen on the other side of the House, including members from the new provinces concerned. I again express the hope that the government will reverse their policy in this respect, and that they will, even at this eleventh hour make some provision for the universities of those two provinces.
Nothing whatever has been done to remove what my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) called the villainous exemption from taxation which is enjoyed by the Canadian Pacific railway throughout Saskatchewan and Alberta. Rightly or wrongly the exemption was given; it was part of the bargain made by the Dominion government for the construction of a great federal undertaking the Canadian Pacific railway and it is not right I siay that all that burden should be placed upon the shoulders of the prairie provinces. In 1905, Mr. Walter Scott the present premier of Saskatchewan made the statement in this House that the Prime Minister had promised him that measures would be taken to remove this unjust exemption from taxation, and although the Prime Minister stated that no such promise had been given he certainly led the House to understand that the government would take some steps to remove this injustice. I hope that the Prime Minister will now conclude that the time has come for him to take up the matter and give immediate relief. ,

The reports in connection with the distribution of seed grain in 1908 have now been brought down. It will be remembered that in the early spring of 1908 the government decided to make a distribution of seed grain to the settlers of Alberta and Saskatchewan who were suffering from the want of seed grain because of a frost which had visited certain sections. The government delayed action most unduly in my opinion, and great expense was caused by this delay as a considerable quantity of the seed had been sent out of the country and had to be brought back again at excessive cost. The price was so high and the conditions so onerous that a number of. the settlers, although they were absolutely without seed, decided they would not accept it, and so a considerable quantity remained in the hands of the government and had in. be disposed of at a loss of over $100,000, although at the same time certain settlers who wanted seed grain had to go without it. The opposition at the time called the attention of the government to the onerous nature of the conditions which they proposed and moved that the payment for the seed grain should not be insisted upon within one year as the government had proposed. Every Conservative member voted that at least two years should be given to the settlers to make payment, but I regret to say that every Liberal member voted against that proposal. The result was that although the value of the grain supplied by the government amounted to $401,027 within the one year specified by the government, only $28,118 had been paid back by the settlers. This shows how absurd the provision insisted upon by the government was, and it also shows what a lever was placed in the hands of the supporters of the government during the election which took place shortly afterwards who told the settlers that if they voted for Liberal candidates they would take care the government would not insist on payment for the grain within one year.
For the last two years the members on this side of the House have been urging upon the government a measure which the grain growers of the Northwest consider to be of vital importance to their industry. We have asked that the government should operate the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. In this connection my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. SchaffneT) moved last year:
That it is the opinion of this House the present system of operating terminal and transfer elevators is detrimental to the interests of the western grain producer, and that the government should take immediate steps to operate the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur and the transfer elevators between these terminals and the Atlantic sea-board.
That resolution was opposed by the members on the other side of the House and was not carried. Since then new conditions have arisen:	The government of
Manitoba has agreed to introduce a Bill establishing a line of internal grain elevators as a public utility, owned by the public and operated by the public. The legislature of Saskatchewan has accepted the same principle. This means that so far as the elevators at initial points are concerned the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan have promised to provide such elevators under government ownership and operation. Now, a great deal of the benefits which will undoubtedly be derived by the grain growers of the west from the policy of the local governments will be lost unless the Dominion government is prepared to implement that by taking over the operation of the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. I would prefer to see the federal government own these elevators, but it has been pointed out that it would involve a very large initial expenditure. I understand, however, that both the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway companies have stated that they are prepared to let the government operate their elevators. I have no doubt that the owners of the other elevators would also agree to the proposal. So that the bugbear of finding a large sum of money to purchase these elevators outright need not stand in the way of the government taking them over, paying a rent for them, and operating them in the interests of the grain growers of the Northwest.
I notice that- the government are bringing in Bills to amend the Grain and Inspection Acts in some minor details. I am prepared to agree that a considerable amount has been done of recent years in the way of improving these Acts, but they are not yet perfect, and I would earnestly commend to the Minister of Trade and Commerce certain proposals which were made at a meeting of the grain growers of Manitoba recently held in the city of Brandon for the amendment of the Grain and Inspection Acts. They are comparatively small matters and yet they are matters of very great importance to the grain growers of this country and I trust that we shall see most of them embodied in the Bills which the government now have before the House. The grain growers are a wideawake, useful and a most able body of men, and I have been impressed by the splendid -work that they have done at the conventions. The very high order of thinking and the high order of speaking that one hears at these conventions show that they are thoroughly imbued with a desire to promote the interests of the grain growers of that country. I trust that the very greatest consideration will be paid to the

proposals which they have made in regard to the important Acts which especially concern our interests in the prairie provinces.

There is another matter which I wish to bring to the notice of the government-another problem which I wish them to take in hand and endeavour to solve. It is not very difficult of solution, and if they will try to live up to the character given them this afternoon by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Schell), they should certainly be able to provide a solution by a wave of their magic wand. I refer to the question of providing harvest help to the Northwest. That is a very serious question indeed. During the past harvest, we had most excellent weather and every facility for getting in the crop; and yet the difficulties in the way of procuring help were so great that it was only by tilt narrowest margin we got that crop saved before the winter set in. We have had an enormous growth throughout the Northwest, and there can be no doubt that the expansion is likely to increase in the near future, but unless some arrangement be made for a . better supply of harvest help, that development is likely to be cut short. If people grow crops and then find it impossible to save them, they will not continue to increase their acreage, which would be a great set-back to the country. I would, therefore, most earnestly recommend the government to take this matter into their consideration. Up to the present it has been left entirely to the railway companies and to private enterprise and it is time the government took hold of it. If they cannot find a means of meeting the difficulty, they should appoint a commission to find out some way by which help can be obtained during the brief period of harvesting. I haye had several suggestions made to me in the Northwest, but I do not think it necessary to enumerate them -at present as there will be abundant suggestions if the government take up the inquiry, as I trust they will in the very near future.
My h-on. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has been held up to us just now by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Schell) as the greatest Minister of Agriculture we have ever had. The minister has, -according to my hon. friend, performed such great prodigies that I have no hesitation in asking him to perform one more, and that is to -do something to put our cattle industry on a better basis. I am speaking more particularly of the cattle industry in the Northwest. I have been a very long time in that -country and have1 seen the cattle industry there in a very flourishing condition, but for several years
past it has been steadily going down hill, and it is time the government did something to put it on a better footing. For many years past the Minister of Agriculture has taken no steps whatever to have the cattle embargo removed by the mother country. He has taken, as far -as I can learn, and as far -as answers given in the British House of Commons indicate, no step whatever during many years* past to have that embargo removed. The ministers in the old country ought to be very friendly to the hon. gentleman and no doubt should be anxious to do something in return for the indirect assistance he has given them. It was our minister who, by his utterances to a great extent, let them out of the preferential tariff difficulty. He made the statement that the farmers of this country did not desire any preferential treatment for their products in the markets of the old world. That was -a -statement which w-as certainly made use of by the ministers in the old -country. It w'as very useful to them when the colonial prime ministers were endeavouring, at the conference of 1907 to obtain some concessions from the mother -country in that respect. If the Minister of Agriculture is not able to prevail on the English government to remove that cattle embargo, he ought to turn his attention to some other means of getting our beef products marketed in a better condition in the mother country.
We had a disquisition this afternoon on the question of surpluses. Well, we are a practical people, and when we -spend more money than we earn, we call the difference a deficit. They do the same thing in Great Britain and the United States. Why -should we depart from that common sense policy and try to make out that we are having surpluses when, as a matter of fact, we -are having deficits from year to year. I am very glad that the Finance Minister adopted the recommendation from this side -at the last session -of parliament, and charged the armaments of our militia and the expenditure on the Dominion land surveys t-o consolidated fund account instead -of to capital account. They should be charged to consolidated fund account instead -of to capital account, as is done at present. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to answer either the criticisms or suggestions which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) has offered to this House this afternoon. I believe, however, that I should devote one or two observations to some of the subjects he has touched upon. The greater part of the hon. member's address has been devoted to questions largely pertaining to the country which he represents particularly in this House, and, as I claim no special authority to discuss these subjects, I shall not follow him upon that ground. The hon. member prefaced his observations with a reference to the question which now occupies the attention of the whole country, the question of naval defence. If I remember his words correctly, he expressed his hearty concurrence in the policy adopted by this government.
No.

I understood him to -say that-the principle of coming to the rescue of the mother country was the right principle, but the government was not going far enough, and should do a great deal more. That is the way I understood the hon. member.	[DOT]
That is right. I did not understand the hon. gentleman's meaning.

That is what I was coming to. I must say that I do not entirely share the views of the hon. gentleman; and I will not surprise any one in this House by say that I propose, in all earnestness and sincerity, to support the policy propounded by the government. It is my belief that this policy is based upon a sound principle, that it is an application of a principle which is common to every one, which is in the heart of every one, the principle of self-defence. But I do not propose to give my views on that subject to any extent, because I shall have an opportunity of doing so on the second reading of the Naval Defence Bill.
The hon. gentleman has also referred to another subject which I consider of vital interest to this country, he has touched upon the construction of the Hudson Bay

railway. I really cannot understand the criticism of the hon. gentleman, after the position taken by this government upon that question. Now, Sir, I propose to make some general observations upon some of the features of the document which is called the budget speech. About tw'o months ago, in this House, an event took place of more than ordinary importance for the representatives of the people and for the entire country. In the fulfilment of a constitutional duty, with his accustomed eloquence, the Minister of Finance, as administrator of the finances of Canada, gave a solemn account of the national assets and liabilities of our Dominion. Even as men of precaution, so Canada needs each year to be posted on the true financial standing, the extent of her obligations and possibilities, so as to safely prepare for future contingencies; and it is the business of the Finance Minister to make known, clearly, loyally and exactly the situation.

ister and the government to which he belongs.

That duty has been well performed and, moreover, by their votes in 1908, the Canadian people have done ample justice to the subject. But as the budget speech sets forth, in a proud and defiant manner, the admirable economic status of Canada, I desire to take advantage of the latitude allowed in this debate to briefly indicate the general effects of the government's policy as far as concerns the advancement and progress of the Dominion. Undeniable is the general and pheno-minal development of Canada under the Liberal government. But the contrast between this condition and the state of stagnation under the Conservative regime is calculated to afford subject matter for serious reflection to our friends opposite. Still, instead of taking a lesson and reforming their party, our friends to the left lose themselves in fruitless recriminations which constitute the main feature of their criticisms. Here are the leading samples: Canada's progress cannot be denied, they say, but that progress is the result of the general economic laws that are felt even in a more pronounced manner in all countries. Or else: Canada's development is fictitious, since our foreign trade shows an ever increasing balance against us. Or else: No matter how great that prosperity, the government has no hand in it, or, in any case, it is but the application of the policy and methods of administration taken from the old regime.
I do not now intend to dwell on all that is specious, contradictory and ill-founded in these arguments of the opposition. But I desire to give them an indirect answer and I invite your attention to those two propositions: .
1.	Since 1896 has Canada grown in proportion to the aspirations of its people?
2.	Is that advancement absolutely foreign to the action of the public authorities, or, on the contrary, is it due in a certain degree to that influence?
1. To the first question statistics reply in the affirmative.
In every sense Canada's economic situation has been a revelation to the world. On this score our country to-day holds a model place, the envy of all civilized nations. Apart from the fluctuation of population, it is agreed that the best barometer of a country's material progress is the position of its leading industries, the volume of its trade, and the condition of its working classes. What does that barometer indicate for us? According to the Minister of Finance, Canada will soon have a population of seven millions. This increase of prosperity, inasmuch as it is the two-fold) result of a regular repatriation of our people from the United States and an increased immigration of the best elements. Men do not seek homes in a coun-

try that is economically depressed and without a national future.
Agriculture is the fundamental source of Canada's prosperity. I've never yet heard any serious denial of this fact. Abundance, comfort, happiness and even wealth in our agricultural classes constitute a fact unprecedented in our annals. The law of supply and demand acts in their favour in a most marvellous manner, until through the increasing value of their products, they have become almost a privileged class in the community.
